posts.text: Agentic AI, explained on one whiteboard. Most people use "agents" as a buzzword. The board breaks it into 5 levels, and each level contains everything to its left. Level 1 is traditional machine learning. Learning patterns from data to make predictions, like a model that prices houses. Level 2 is enhanced ML. Same models, better results, through feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, cross-validation, and ensembles. Level 3 is intelligent applications. Models deployed in real products with context and feedback. Real-time inference, data pipelines, monitoring, A/B testing. Think recommendation systems. Level 4 is autonomous agents. Systems that make decisions and act with limited human intervention. The core loop is perceive, decide, act, backed by goal setting, memory, and environment interaction. An auto-trading bot lives here. Level 5 is agentic systems. Fully autonomous systems that plan, learn, and pursue complex goals across domains. The loop upgrades to plan, execute, reflect, learn. Strategic planning, multi-step reasoning, tool use, self-improvement. An AI research assistant is the canonical example. Two things apply at every level. The principles nobody gets to skip. Safety, ethics, privacy, transparency, human in the loop. And the enablers nobody gets to skip either. Data quality, compute, MLOps, evals, and the talent to run it all. Success is simple to define. The system solves real problems, adapts to change, creates value, improves over time, and stays aligned with human goals. To go deeper: • AI Foundations for PMs: https://lnkd.in/e6zyYugs • AI Agents for PMs: https://lnkd.in/eeey5Cxr • Practical AI Agents: https://lnkd.in/eyamsW7a The whole board comes down to one line at the bottom. The goal was never just smarter models. Smarter systems win.

posts.text: +80.8%, then -70%. I used to think more agents meant an upgrade. But then I found this research. A controlled study tested 260 configurations, across 6 benchmarks and 5 architectures. On the right kind of task, multi-agent improved performance by 80.8%. On the wrong kind, it killed performance by 70%. And the difference wasn't coming from the technology. But whether the task could actually be split up, or not. There is something even more interesting. When agents work independently, with nobody checking their output, errors got amplified 17.2x. Add just one check of their work and that dropped to 4.4x. Just because someone started checking. The cost side problem is also serious. Anthropic: A single agent uses about 4x the tokens of a normal chat. A multi-agent system uses about 15x. Run that at 10,000 tasks a month, and the gap is hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. I don't want to scare you. Or to make you think that you should never use more than one agent. It is just not always that easy to choose if you need one or many. I've found a study where a multi-agent system was 94% cheaper than a single agent. And even more accurate. It used cheaper models for the easy parts, instead of running everything through the expensive one. That's why your choice between one or many should be economic, not aesthetic. Don't make the decision based on instinct. So I put together 7 mistakes that cause this decision to go wrong. Don't make them like most and you will save a ton. PS: have you ever added an agent because it felt more advanced?

posts.text: 🤖 Autonomous Multi-Agent Healthcare Orchestration on AWS How can payers and providers use Amazon Bedrock Agents, AgentCore, MCP, and secure tool-calling to coordinate healthcare workflows in parallel? Healthcare workflows often require eligibility checks, clinical validation, prior authorization, claims analysis, compliance review, and policy retrieval. Running everything sequentially is slow. Parallel delegation can reduce workflow latency and improve operational efficiency. 🏗️ The Architecture User Request → Orchestrator Agent → Delegated Agents → MCP Tools → Enterprise Systems → Results → Validation → Final Response The Orchestrator coordinates specialized agents: 🔹 Eligibility Agent → Coverage and benefits 🔹 Clinical Agent → Guidelines and medical necessity 🔹 Claims Agent → Authorization and claims rules 🔹 Compliance Agent → Privacy and policy checks 🔹 RAG Agent → Payer policies and clinical knowledge 🔹 Provider Agent → NPI and network validation ⚡ Parallel Execution Example Request: “Does this patient qualify for MRI prior authorization?” The Orchestrator delegates tasks: Eligibility Agent: Verify coverage Clinical Agent: Evaluate clinical criteria Claims Agent: Check authorization requirements RAG Agent: Retrieve current payer policies Compliance Agent: Validate access and handling requirements Each agent returns a structured result: Agent → Task → Evidence → Decision → Confidence → Risk → Next Action The Orchestrator aggregates the results and determines whether to recommend approval, request more information, or escalate to a qualified human reviewer. 🔐 Where AWS + MCP Fit Amazon Bedrock Agents: Model-driven task execution and tool use. AgentCore: Runtime, identity, memory, gateway, and multi-agent capabilities, where supported by the selected AgentCore services. MCP: A standardized interface for connecting agents to authorized tools and enterprise systems. GitHub + FHIR + SQL + APIs: Potential sources of versioned policies, clinical knowledge, and operational data. Every tool call should enforce identity, least privilege, PHI controls, authorization, auditability, and result validation. ⚠️ Important: Parallel execution does not automatically make decisions faster or safer. Use deterministic orchestration, bounded delegation, and human approval for high-impact clinical and financial actions. 💼 Why It Matters One orchestrator. Multiple specialized agents. Coordinated execution. The result: ⚡ Faster administrative workflows 🔐 Stronger security boundaries 📋 Better auditability 📈 Scalable payer and provider operations 🤝 More efficient human decision-making The future of healthcare AI is not just smarter models. It's secure, observable, multi-agent orchestration that turns enterprise data into coordinated action. hashtag #AgenticAI hashtag #AIAgents hashtag #AWS hashtag #AmazonBedrock hashtag #BedrockAgents hashtag #AgentCore hashtag #MCP hashtag #HealthcareAI hashtag #FHIR hashtag #RAG hashtag #AISecurity hashtag #AIArchitecture hashtag #LLMOps hashtag #CloudSecurity #HealthcareAI#EnterpriseAI hashtag #AIGovernance hashtag #MultiAgent

posts.text: 🤖 Agentic AI isn't just a buzzword — it's a completely different way of building with LLMs. Most people still think of AI as "type a prompt, get an answer." Agentic AI flips that. Instead of one input → one output, an agent runs a loop: Perceive → Plan → Act → Observe → Reflect It decides what to do next, calls tools, reads the results, and adjusts — often without a human steering every step. A few concepts worth knowing if you're getting into this space: → Memory — agents need short-term context AND long-term memory (episodic + semantic) to stay coherent across steps→ Tool use — function calling is what turns a text generator into something that can actually search, code, and take action→ ReAct & Reflexion — reasoning patterns where agents interleave thinking with acting, and even critique their own attempts → Multi-agent systems — complex work gets split across specialized agents (orchestrator + workers), just like a human team The exciting part? We're still early. The frameworks (LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen) and best practices are evolving fast, and the gap between "demo" and "reliable production agent" is where most of the real engineering work is happening right now. Curious what others are building with agents — drop your favorite use case or framework below 👇 hashtag #AgenticAI hashtag #ArtificialIntelligence hashtag #LLM hashtag #AIagents hashtag #MachineLearning

posts.text: AI is entering production faster than enterprises are building the ability to observe, govern and control it. Traditional observability answers: “Is my system healthy?” But with LLMs, RAG, AI Agents and autonomous workflows, enterprises need to ask a much harder question: “Is my AI behaving correctly, safely, efficiently and within policy?” That is why I believe Enterprise AI Observability is becoming a critical capability. The emerging stack is evolving across 5 layers: 1) Traditional Observability Infrastructure, applications, logs, metrics, traces, latency and performance — the foundation. 2) AI Observability Prompt/response tracing, token usage, LLM performance, RAG quality, hallucinations, agent/tool calls, evaluations, model drift and cost. 3) AI Governance & Runtime Control Policy enforcement, model governance, risk, compliance, auditability and agent governance. 4) AI Runtime Security Prompt injection, data leakage, malicious tool calls, agent abuse, MCP security and unauthorized model access. 5) AI Production Management AI SRE, Agent Operations, AI FinOps, incident & change management, agent identity, AI service catalog and reliability. The bigger shift is: Infrastructure Observability → Application Observability → AI Observability → AI Production Management And the winning platforms won't just tell us whether an AI system is running. They will tell us whether it is: Reliable. Accurate. Secure. Compliant. Cost-efficient. Explainable. Most importantly: Can we operate AI at enterprise scale with the same confidence with which we operate our most critical business systems? That, in my view, is the next frontier of enterprise AI. AI doesn't just need to be intelligent. It needs to be observable, governable, secure and operable. posts.text: Most demos of multi-agent AI focus on getting agents to collaborate. In healthcare, I kept running into the opposite problem, agents that agree too easily. Ask several language models to discuss a case and they tend to converge on whatever the first confident voice said. The output looks like consensus. It's often just an echo, and in a clinical setting, a panel that agrees quickly can look far more trustworthy than it actually is. That gap, between the appearance of deliberation and the real thing, is what I wanted to engineer around. I have built a prototype that treats disagreement as the point rather than a failure to smooth over. The core idea is that healthy dissent doesn't emerge on its own, you have to design a role that produces it. So one agent's entire job is to challenge the group when it settles too comfortably, but only when there's a genuine, detectable reason to doubt the majority. The design question underneath it generalizes well beyond healthcare, a multi-agent system is only as good as its ability to notice when it's about to be confidently wrong. Code and a full write-up in the comments. 👇

posts.text: We may be creating more AI experts than AI results. I’m seeing an interesting phenomenon on LinkedIn. Every day there is another AI lifecycle. Another AI framework. Another “enterprise AI stack.” Another diagram showing agents, RAG, MCP, vector databases, orchestration, governance and 20 different tools. And apparently, knowing how to arrange those boxes now makes someone an AI strategist. Maybe I’m being overly critical—but after spending decades in IT, I think we’re missing something. Technology expertise isn’t the ability to describe technology. It’s the ability to make technology work in the real world. I’ve seen this movie before. We had ERP experts who knew every module but couldn’t get the business process right. Data experts who could build beautiful dashboards from questionable data. Cloud experts who moved workloads to the cloud without changing the economics. And now we’re seeing AI experts who can explain agents for 30 minutes—but may never have had to convince a CFO that the investment actually creates value. Enterprise AI isn’t primarily a model problem. It isn’t even primarily a tooling problem. It’s a business problem. Before asking “Which AI framework should we use?”, I’d rather ask: • What decision are we trying to improve? • What process are we trying to change? • Is our data good enough? • What happens when the AI is wrong? • Who is accountable? • What does this save or generate? • Can the organization actually adopt it? And perhaps the most important question: Would we still build this if we removed the word “AI” from the conversation? Because sometimes the answer is automation. Sometimes it’s better data. Sometimes it’s process redesign. Sometimes it’s traditional analytics. And sometimes, absolutely, it’s AI. That’s the distinction I see between AI literacy and AI leadership. You don’t need to know every new AI tool to lead an AI transformation. You need to understand the business, the technology, the data, the economics, the people and the risk—and know where AI genuinely belongs. The winners in enterprise AI won’t be those who can name the most frameworks. They’ll be those who can turn AI into measurable business outcomes. hashtag #EnterpriseAI hashtag #AILeadership hashtag #CIO hashtag #CTO hashtag #DigitalTransformation

posts.text: A lot of people are scared of AI right now. They talk about AI like it is alive or unpredictable, but AI is not magic. AI is nothing without the records and the information that feed it. If the records are ungoverned, the behavior becomes unpredictable. If the records are governed, the behavior becomes controlled. Here is the formula: Governance Metadata + Enforcement Rules = Governed AI Governance metadata are the labels that tell AI what the information is, and how it must be treated. Enforcement rules are the instructions that tell AI what to do, and what not to do. When every record carries both, the entire system becomes a controlled environment. If every record inside an AI system is governed, the data is governed. If the data is governed, the information is governed. If the information is governed, the model is governed. AI cannot act outside the boundaries of the records it learns from. No structure means unpredictability. Unpredictability creates fear. Structure removes unpredictability. Structure removes fear. If structure is the key to controlling AI, AI does not need to be feared.

posts.text: Is your product catalog optimized for Agentic AI? Because soon, your first customer may not be human. Gartner forecasts that 90% of B2B purchases could be handled by AI agents within the next three years, potentially channeling over $15 trillion through automated exchanges. And this isn't just a B2B story. McKinsey estimates that Agentic Commerce could orchestrate $3 trillion to $5 trillion in B2C spending globally by 2030. So here's the question businesses should be asking: Will an AI agent be able to find, understand and choose your product? Because the buying journey is about to change. Machine-to-machine buying An AI agent identifies suppliers, compares products and places orders. Zero-click workflows No browsing through pages. No reading through PDFs. Just structured data flowing between systems. And the biggest risk: invisibility Your product can be better, cheaper, even more relevant but if the agent cannot understand it, it may never show up as an option. O'Reilly ran a simple experiment that illustrates it vividly. An AI agent was asked to find a waterproof jacket. It picked the more expensive one ten out of ten times. The cheaper jacket had great copy: "Ultra-breathable all-weather shell. Conquers stormy seas." The expensive one simply had: water_resistance_mm: 20000 The agent needed a specification number to make the "waterproof" decision. It couldn't turn marketing copy into one. So the cheaper product was filtered out. I have seen versions of this problem before. I worked on catalog quality at Rakuten with 20Mn+ SKUs. Sellers had titles, PDFs and product images but they often didn't have complete, structured product data. Back then, it affected search, discovery and conversion. With AI agents becoming the first layer of discovery, the stakes are different.A missing attribute is no longer just a catalog quality issue. It could decide whether your product even enters the consideration set. We spent years optimizing product pages for humans.The next challenge is optimizing product data for machines. And I think many businesses haven't fully started preparing for that shift yet. Is catalog and product data quality being discussed as an AI strategy in your organization? Or is it still just a data hygiene problem for someone else to fix?

posts.text: When I left IBM, I knew I didn’t want to spend the next chapter of my career simply talking about AI—or even just designing and building algorithms for large corporations. I wanted to build something that could actually move the needle. For more than 30 years, I’ve built and deployed AI solutions for large organizations. I also served four years on IBM’s AI Ethics Board and became a leading voice on responsible AI, algorithmic bias, and the harm these systems can create. I didn’t come to this issue only through research. I completed my PhD in Artificial Intelligence with research focused on algorithmic bias and real-world harm. I also wrote Hidden in White Sight, examining how bias can become embedded in the technologies and systems shaping people’s lives. But my perspective has never been purely academic. It has been shaped by decades of actually building and deploying the kinds of systems we are now being asked to govern. That led me to an uncomfortable reality: The value organizations see in building and deploying AI will almost always outweigh the perceived risk of the bias or harm that AI might produce. No matter what we believe, advocate for, or warn against, AI adoption is not slowing down. As one technology CEO has said, the horse is already out of the barn. Organizations are not going to stop building AI. Nor should they. The real question is whether we will build the accountability and safeguards necessary to understand what these systems are doing—and address the harm when they get it wrong. That is why I founded Xtegrity. I brought together a small team of senior technology leaders with experience at IBM, Google, and Microsoft to help turn that vision into a platform designed to change how organizations understand and manage AI risk. Xtegrity moves AI governance beyond policies, checklists, frameworks, and conversations—and toward action. It enables organizations to simulate potential harm before AI causes it, identify and deter harmful outcomes, quantify the financial risk of AI harm, and govern models where they already operate—across clouds and environments—without moving models or sensitive data. Perhaps most importantly to me, Xtegrity creates a pathway for people who believe they have been harmed by AI to identify that harm and connect directly with the organizations responsible for the models. I’ve done a lot of talking. I’ve done a lot of research. I’ve built a lot of technology. But at some point, talking about responsible AI is not enough. We have to build something that makes responsibility real. That is what Xtegrity represents for me. As we build increasingly powerful AI systems, we must also build the mechanisms to understand their risk, anticipate their harm, quantify the consequences—and hold them accountable. Today, I’m introducing Xtegrity to the world. Over the next few weeks, we’ll share more about the platform and our official launch event. This is what we’ve built
